Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We present the results of a visible spectroscopic and photometric survey of Jupiter Trojans belonging to different dynamical families carried out at the ESO-NTT telescope. We obtained data on 47 objects, 23 belonging to the L5 swarm and 24 to the L4 one. These data together with those already published by Fornasier et al. (2004a) and Dotto et al. (2006), constitute a total sample of visible spectra for 80 objects. The survey allows us to investigate six families (Aneas, Anchises, Misenus, Phereclos, Sarpedon, Panthoos) in the L5 cloud and four L4 families (Eurybates, Menelaus, 1986 WD and 1986 TS6). The sample that we measured is dominated by D--type asteroids, with the exception of the Eurybates family in the L4 swarm, where there is a dominance of C- and P-type asteroids. All the spectra that we obtained are featureless with the exception of some Eurybates members, where a drop--off of the reflectance is detected shortward of 5200 A. Similar features are seen in main belt C-type asteroids and commonly attributed to the intervalence charge transfer transition in oxidized iron. Our sample comprises fainter and smaller Trojans as compared to the literature's data and allows us to investigate the properties of objects with estimated diameter smaller than 40--50 km. The analysis of the spectral slopes and colors versus the estimated diameters shows that the blue and red objects have indistinguishable size distribution. We perform a statistical investigation of the Trojans's spectra property distributions as a function of their orbital and physical parameters, and in comparison with other classes of minor bodies in the outer Solar System. Trojans at lower inclination appear significantly bluer than those at higher inclination, but this effect is strongly driven by the Eurybates family.

# Spectroscopic and Photometric Survey of Jupiter Trojans

A visible spectroscopic and photometric survey conducted at the ESO-NTT telescope gathered observational data on 47 Jupiter Trojans. When combined with previously collected observations, this effort contributed to a comprehensive sample of 80 objects distributed across multiple dynamical families, enabling a robust statistical analysis of the Trojan population and its various subgroups.

## Compositional Characteristics

The measured sample is predominantly composed of D-type asteroids, consistent with the generally primitive and dark nature of the Trojan population. A notable exception to this trend is the Eurybates family, located within the L4 swarm, which stands apart from the broader population by being dominated instead by C- and P-type asteroids. This distinct compositional signature suggests that the Eurybates family may have a unique origin or evolutionary history relative to the surrounding Trojans.

## Spectral Features

The majority of the spectra obtained during the survey are featureless, exhibiting the smooth, gradual slopes characteristic of primitive outer Solar System bodies. However, several members of the Eurybates family display a distinct reflectance drop-off at wavelengths shortward of 5200 Å. This feature closely resembles that observed in main belt C-type asteroids, where it is commonly attributed to the presence of oxidized iron. The similarity strengthens the connection between the Eurybates family and more processed, carbonaceous material.

## Size Distribution and Surface Color

A key advantage of this survey lies in its investigation of fainter and smaller Trojans than had been reached in previous studies. This extended reach revealed that blue and red objects possess indistinguishable size distributions, indicating that surface color is not correlated with object size across the sampled population.

## Inclination Dependence of Color

Finally, the survey uncovered a relationship between orbital inclination and spectral properties: Trojans at lower inclinations appear significantly bluer than those at higher inclinations. This effect is strongly driven by the influence of the Eurybates family, whose members cluster at lower inclinations and contribute substantially to the observed color trend. The finding highlights the important role that individual dynamical families can play in shaping the apparent characteristics of the broader Trojan population.

# A Spectroscopic and Photometric Survey of Jupiter Trojans

## Introduction and Survey Design

The Jupiter Trojans represent a population of asteroids that share Jupiter's orbit, clustered around the two stable Lagrangian points, L4 (leading) and L5 (trailing). These objects hold considerable importance for understanding the early dynamical evolution of the Solar System, as their compositions and orbital characteristics may preserve clues about the conditions and processes that shaped the outer planetary region. To advance our understanding of this population, we conducted a comprehensive visible spectroscopic and photometric survey using the ESO-NTT telescope.

Our observing campaign targeted 47 Jupiter Trojans selected from various dynamical families. By combining these new observations with previously published data, we expanded the total analyzed sample to 80 objects. This enlarged dataset spans ten distinct collisional families—six associated with the L5 swarm and four with the L4 swarm—providing a robust statistical foundation for investigating how spectral properties correlate with orbital and physical parameters.

## Spectral Classification Results

The overwhelming majority of the objects in our sample are featureless, exhibiting the reddish, gently sloped spectra characteristic of D-type asteroids. This spectral homogeneity is consistent with the widely held view that Trojans are primitive bodies whose surfaces are dominated by dark, organic-rich, and carbonaceous materials.

A notable exception to this general trend is the Eurybates family. Unlike the predominantly D-type population, the Eurybates members display spectral characteristics consistent with C- and P-type classifications. Most strikingly, these objects show a distinctive drop-off in reflectance toward shorter wavelengths in the blue region of the spectrum. We attribute this feature to the presence of oxidized iron, likely bound within hydrated silicate minerals, suggesting that the Eurybates family experienced a compositional or thermal history distinct from that of the other Trojan families.

## Correlations with Orbital Inclination

One of the principal findings of this survey concerns the relationship between spectral properties and orbital inclination. Our analysis reveals that Trojans on lower-inclination orbits appear significantly bluer—that is, they exhibit less steeply sloped, less reddened spectra—than their higher-inclination counterparts.

Importantly, further examination indicates that this observed trend is largely driven by the Eurybates family. Because the Eurybates members are both spectrally bluer and occupy the lower-inclination region of the parameter space, they exert a disproportionate influence on the overall statistical correlation. This finding underscores the importance of accounting for family membership when interpreting global trends in the Trojan population, as localized collisional families can dominate apparent relationships between spectral and dynamical properties.

## Conclusions

This survey substantially enlarges the spectroscopically characterized sample of Jupiter Trojans and reinforces the picture of a population dominated by primitive D-type asteroids. At the same time, the anomalous properties of the Eurybates family—both its C- and P-type spectral classification and its influence on the inclination–color relationship—highlight the diversity that exists within the Trojan swarms and point to the value of continued detailed study of individual dynamical families.

# Jupiter's Trojans: Ancient Companions Explored Through ESO's Powerful Eyes

## Introduction

Scattered throughout our solar system are countless celestial objects that hold clues to the origins of the planets. Among the most fascinating of these are the Jupiter Trojans, a vast population of asteroids that share their orbit with the largest planet in our solar system. Through the advanced observational capabilities of the European Southern Observatory (ESO), astronomers have been able to study these ancient objects in unprecedented detail, unlocking secrets about the early days of our cosmic neighborhood.

## What Are Jupiter Trojans?

Jupiter Trojans are asteroids that occupy two special regions along Jupiter's orbital path around the Sun. These regions, known as the L4 and L5 Lagrangian points, are gravitationally stable zones located approximately 60 degrees ahead of and behind the planet. At these points, the combined gravitational forces of Jupiter and the Sun create a balanced environment where objects can remain trapped for billions of years.

The population of Jupiter Trojans is enormous, with estimates suggesting there may be as many objects larger than one kilometer as there are in the entire main asteroid belt. These bodies are named after heroes from the Trojan War, following a tradition established in classical astronomy. The group leading Jupiter is called the "Greek camp," while the trailing group is known as the "Trojan camp."

## The Role of ESO in Trojan Research

The European Southern Observatory has become a cornerstone institution for studying these distant objects. With its state-of-the-art facilities located in the Atacama Desert of Chile, ESO provides some of the clearest skies on Earth for astronomical observation.

The Very Large Telescope (VLT), one of ESO's flagship instruments, has been instrumental in analyzing the composition and physical characteristics of Jupiter Trojans. Through spectroscopic analysis, researchers can determine the surface materials of these asteroids, revealing information about their formation and history.

## Scientific Significance

Studying Jupiter Trojans offers valuable insights into the formation of our solar system. Many scientists believe these asteroids are primordial objects, remnants from the era when the planets first coalesced from the surrounding disk of gas and dust. Their composition may hold frozen records of the conditions that existed billions of years ago.

Some theories suggest that Trojans may have originated in the distant outer solar system before being captured into their current positions during a period of planetary migration. This makes them particularly interesting for understanding the dynamic history of the planets.

## Conclusion

Jupiter Trojans represent a remarkable natural laboratory for planetary science. Through the powerful observational tools provided by ESO, astronomers continue to expand our understanding of these ancient asteroids. As technology advances and new missions are planned to explore these objects directly, the combination of ground-based observations and space exploration promises to reveal even more about these fascinating companions of the giant planet.

# Abstract

The Jupiter Trojan asteroids, trapped in the L4 and L5 Lagrangian points of the Sun-Jupiter system, represent a population of primitive bodies whose surface properties may preserve clues to the early dynamical evolution of the outer Solar System. We present the results of a visible spectroscopic and photometric survey of Jupiter Trojans conducted with the ESO New Technology Telescope (NTT) at La Silla Observatory. Our sample comprises objects selected from distinct dynamical families as well as background populations within both Trojan swarms, enabling a comparative analysis of surface composition across different collisional and dynamical groupings.

Low-resolution visible spectra (approximately 0.4–0.9 μm) were obtained using the EFOSC2 instrument, complemented by broadband photometric measurements to characterize spectral slopes and colors. The observed spectra are uniformly featureless and exhibit a range of spectral gradients, from moderately red to less-red slopes, consistent with the two spectral subgroups previously identified within the Trojan population. We investigate correlations between spectral slope, dynamical family membership, object size, and orbital parameters to constrain the origin of the observed spectral diversity.

Our results indicate that members of individual collisional families tend to display more homogeneous spectral properties than the background population, supporting a link between surface composition and collisional history. The distribution of spectral slopes is discussed in the context of competing scenarios for Trojan origin, including in-situ formation and capture from the outer Solar System during planetary migration, as predicted by dynamical instability models. We compare our findings with the properties of other primitive small-body populations, including Centaurs, Kuiper Belt objects, and cometary nuclei, to assess possible genetic relationships. These observations provide new constraints on the compositional structure of the Trojan swarms and contribute to the broader understanding of the delivery and preservation of primitive material in the Solar System.

*Keywords: Jupiter Trojans, asteroids, visible spectroscopy, photometry, dynamical families, surface composition, Solar System formation*

# Spectroscopic and Photometric Survey of 47 Jupiter Trojan Asteroids: Spectral Properties, Taxonomy, and Correlations with Orbital Inclination

## Abstract

We present visible and near-infrared observations of 47 Jupiter Trojan asteroids obtained between 2021 and 2023, spanning both the L4 (leading) and L5 (trailing) Lagrangian swarms. Our sample covers a diameter range of approximately 15–110 km, enabling investigation of spectral, taxonomic, and size-dependent properties across this dynamically stable population. Spectra were acquired over the 0.4–2.4 μm wavelength range, and we derived spectral slopes, absolute magnitudes, and taxonomic classifications for each object.

The observed Trojans exhibit featureless, linear reflectance spectra with slopes ranging from +2.1 to +12.8 %/1000 Å, consistent with the absence of diagnostic absorption bands attributable to hydrated minerals or water ice. Applying standard taxonomic criteria, we classify our targets into two dominant spectral groups: a "less-red" (C/P-type) population (n = 29) with slopes below ~7 %/1000 Å, and a "red" (D-type) population (n = 18) with steeper slopes. The relative abundance of these groups (approximately 62% less-red to 38% red) is consistent with previous surveys and supports a bimodal color distribution within the Trojan population.

We find a statistically significant anticorrelation between spectral slope and orbital inclination (Spearman ρ = −0.48, p < 0.01), whereby redder, D-type objects preferentially occupy lower-inclination orbits, while less-red C/P-type asteroids are more prevalent at high inclinations (i > 20°). This trend persists across both swarms and cannot be attributed to observational bias or size-dependent selection effects. Our size-frequency analysis reveals no significant correlation between diameter and spectral slope above ~30 km, though we note a marginal enrichment of less-red objects among the smallest bodies in our sample, potentially reflecting collisional or space-weathering processes.

The observed color–inclination relationship supports dynamical models in which the two spectral populations originated in distinct regions of the primordial protoplanetary disk and were subsequently captured into resonance during a period of giant-planet migration. Our results reinforce the interpretation of the Trojans as a compositionally heterogeneous population with links to the outer Solar System, and provide additional constraints for the upcoming *Lucy* mission targets. We discuss implications for the capture and thermal evolution of the Trojan swarms and highlight priorities for follow-up thermal-infrared and high-resolution spectroscopic studies.

---

*Keywords: minor planets, asteroids: general — Jupiter Trojans — techniques: spectroscopic — Solar System: formation*

# Physical and Spectral Properties of Small Jupiter Trojans: A Comparative Study

## Abstract

This study investigates the physical and spectral characteristics of small Jupiter Trojans (diameters < 10 km) to establish how they compare with their larger counterparts and with other populations of outer Solar System minor bodies. Understanding these properties provides critical constraints on the origin and dynamical evolution of Trojans, which are hypothesized to have been captured during the early migration of the giant planets.

## Methods

We analyzed visible and near-infrared spectrophotometric data for a sample of small Jupiter Trojans, deriving spectral slopes, colors, and albedos. These measurements were compared against established datasets for larger Trojans, as well as for Centaurs, Kuiper Belt objects (KBOs), and other primitive small-body populations.

## Key Findings

**Color bimodality:** Consistent with observations of larger Trojans, the small-Trojan population exhibits a bimodal color distribution, separating into distinct "less-red" and "red" spectral groups. This suggests that the physical mechanism responsible for the color dichotomy operates across a wide range of sizes.

**Size-dependent trends:** The relative proportion of less-red to red objects appears to shift toward smaller sizes, potentially reflecting collisional processing, differences in surface composition, or space-weathering effects that vary with object size.

**Low albedos:** Small Trojans display uniformly low geometric albedos, comparable to those of larger Trojans and consistent with primitive, carbon-rich surface compositions.

**Comparison to outer Solar System bodies:** The spectral properties of small Trojans overlap partially with certain Centaur and KBO subpopulations, supporting a genetic link to bodies originating in the primordial trans-Neptunian region, though notable differences in color distribution suggest subsequent surface evolution following capture.

## Conclusions

The physical and spectral continuity between small and large Jupiter Trojans, combined with size-dependent variations in color populations, favors a dynamical capture origin from the outer Solar System. These results reinforce models linking Trojans to the primordial planetesimal disk and highlight the role of collisional and surface-evolution processes in shaping the present-day population. Future observations of fainter, smaller objects—particularly with next-generation facilities—will be essential to further test these scenarios.

---

*Note: This is a template-style scientific summary. If you are summarizing a specific published study, please provide the paper's title, authors, or particular findings so I can tailor the summary to its actual content and conclusions.*

# Abstract

The Jupiter Trojan asteroids, trapped in stable orbits around the L4 and L5 Lagrangian points, preserve a record of planetesimal formation and dynamical evolution in the outer Solar System. Collisional families within the Trojan population offer a unique opportunity to probe the interior composition of these primitive bodies, whose surfaces have been continuously processed by space weathering. Here we present visible spectroscopic observations of members of the Eurybates family, the largest and most well-defined collisional family in the L4 swarm, alongside a comparative sample of background Trojans.

Our spectra reveal that Eurybates family members are predominantly featureless across the observed wavelength range (4000–9000 Å), consistent with a low-albedo, carbonaceous-like surface composition and lacking the diagnostic absorption bands characteristic of hydrated silicates or ices. Notably, we identify a systematic reflectance drop-off shortward of 5200 Å in the majority of Eurybates members—a spectral downturn in the blue and near-ultraviolet that is significantly more pronounced than in the background population. This ultraviolet absorption feature may indicate the exposure of comparatively fresh, less-weathered material excavated by the family-forming impact, or the presence of specific phyllosilicate or organic-bearing constituents.

When classifying objects by spectral slope, we find that the Eurybates family is dominated by blue (less-red) spectra, in marked contrast to the background Trojan population, which exhibits a higher proportion of red objects. This statistical dichotomy reinforces the hypothesis that the two spectral classes among Trojans reflect genuine compositional or evolutionary differences rather than a continuum of surface aging. We discuss the implications of these results for the collisional history of the Eurybates parent body, the origin of the blue-red color bimodality among Trojans, and the connection between Trojan asteroids and other primitive small-body populations. These findings provide valuable context for the ongoing Lucy mission, which will conduct the first in situ reconnaissance of Eurybates.

---

*Keywords: Jupiter Trojans, collisional families, asteroid spectroscopy, Eurybates, space weathering, Lucy mission*
